title: The minister who left
hook: Emerson resigned his pulpit, unable in conscience to lead communion as the church required

segments.voice: Yesterday, Montaigne close: a man who tried out his judgment on his own life. Your line was my attempt. What did your short essay turn out to be about? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

A young minister climbs into his pulpit with a sermon he knows will cost him his job. The people in front of him know him well. And he's about to explain, carefully and politely, why he can no longer lead one of the central rites of his church, the Lord's Supper, in the way it asks. He isn't angry. He isn't storming out. He's just found something he can't do with a clear conscience. His name is Ralph Waldo Emerson, and a new block starts with him walking down from that pulpit. Today, the minister who left.
screen: `A SERMON THAT WILL COST HIM.` → `NOT ANGRY. CAREFUL.` → `RALPH WALDO EMERSON.`

segments.voice: First, what was asked of him. In Christian churches, the Lord's Supper, or communion, is a sacred meal, done in memory of Jesus. Churches understand it in different ways, and for those who receive it, it can be at the heart of their faith. Emerson's church expected its minister to lead it. Second, what he came to think. In his farewell sermon, Emerson reads the Gospel accounts closely and argues that Jesus did not mean this meal to be a fixed rite for all time. That's his reading; Christians across the churches have read the same passages very differently, and still do. But Emerson goes further, and the further part is personal. This way of remembering Jesus, he says, no longer suits him, and for him that is reason enough to give it up. Third, how he left. By the usual account, he first asked whether he could stay on without leading the rite. The church said no. So he went. And in the sermon he is careful to say he has no hostility to the practice, and no quarrel with those who find it helpful. He isn't asking anyone to follow him out. Fourth, the cost. A pulpit was his work, his income, his place in the town. He gave it up over one thing he couldn't do honestly. That's what in conscience means: not that you're certainly right, but that you won't stand up in front of people and act out what you don't hold. Most weeks, the stakes are smaller. A meeting where you're asked to agree. A form that wants a yes. The question is the same one Emerson faced: can I do this with a clear conscience?
screen: `THE LORD'S SUPPER, A SACRED MEAL.` · `IT NO LONGER SUITS ME.` · `NO HOSTILITY, NO QUARREL.` · `HE GAVE UP THE PULPIT.` · then, large: `IN CONSCIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one conviction you'd keep at a cost. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Ask yourself quietly: is there something I wouldn't do, or wouldn't pretend, even if it cost me a job, a friendship, a good opinion? It might be large. It might be small, like not laughing at a cruel joke. Don't argue for it. Just find it, and name it in a few words. Then notice how it feels to hold it. The bell holds the time.

The minister who left. Emerson, who stepped down from his pulpit rather than lead a rite he could no longer lead with a clear conscience, and who said he had no quarrel with those who kept it. Today's word.
Your line: in conscience. Today, before you say yes to something, pause long enough to ask whether you can do it with a clear conscience. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often point to his farewell sermon on the Lord's Supper as an example of leaving a role quietly over a matter of conscience, without attacking those who stay.

fork.setup: you're Emerson. you can no longer lead the Lord's Supper with a clear conscience, and your church needs you to. what do you do?
options: lead it anyway and keep quiet.
ask to stay without leading it, and leave when they say no.
preach against communion until they fire you.
fork.reveal: by the usual account he asked to stay without leading it. when the church said no, he gave a careful farewell sermon and stepped down.

trapdoor: what you thought: the minister who left lost his faith and walked out angry.
what it means: Emerson left over one rite he couldn't lead in conscience, and said he had no quarrel with those who kept it.
what a scholar hears: his farewell sermon argues from the Gospel texts, then says the rite no longer suits him, and that this is reason enough.

sources.ref: The Lord's Supper (farewell sermon at the Second Church, Boston): reading of the Gospel accounts; the rite no longer suitable to him, reason enough to abandon it; no hostility to the institution
